description: Somos a equipe Raízes do Futuro, vencedora do Youth Challenge Blockchain 2026 (UNICEF Brasil), com integrantes de diferentes cidades do Brasil. Unimos desenvolvimento web2/web3, IA e design para criar soluções de impacto social e ambiental em comunidades costeiras da Bahia. No Space Apps, queremos usar dados da NASA para entender mudanças no território e transformar isso em informação útil para quem vive lá. Equipe: Milena (líder e dev), Maria Clara (dev) e Amanda Folly (design e pitch).
summary: Raízes do Futuro: Island Trend Detective is a live web tool that turns 45 years of NASA POWER data into four answers for any place on Earth: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. Pick a point on the map and the page calls the NASA POWER API, runs Mann-Kendall tests with autocorrelation correction, Theil-Sen slopes, Pettitt change-point detection and false discovery rate control across neighbouring cells, and explains the result in plain language. It also builds an hourly heat calendar for outdoor work and a downloadable report for any place. We tested it on Boipeba Island, Brazil, where our community recycling project works outdoors. The answer: days when the heat index reaches 32 °C, the level of extreme caution for outdoor work, doubled from 64 to 132 a year, with a shift after 2018. Warming is significant across the whole coast. We turned the hourly heat calendar into a safer collection schedule and flag a possible drying signal openly instead of claiming it. It matters because climate data rarely reaches the small communities that live with it, and this tool works for any of them.
details:
Raízes do Futuro: Island Trend Detective is a live, open web tool. Anyone clicks a place on the map (or types coordinates), chooses a NASA POWER variable (air temperature, daily maximum, rainfall, humidity, wind or solar radiation) and gets four answers in seconds:

  • What is changing: the direction of the trend, in plain language.
  • How much: Theil-Sen slope per decade with a 95% confidence interval, plus first and last decade means.
  • Is it significant: Mann-Kendall test with the Hamed and Rao (1998) correction for autocorrelation.
  • Since when: Pettitt change-point test. "Scan the area" tests 9 neighbouring NASA POWER cells and colours them on the map, with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control, to answer where. "Build heat calendar" downloads 10 years of NASA POWER hourly temperature and humidity for the chosen place, computes the heat index and compares 2001 to 2005 with 2021 to 2025: how many days reach 32 °C (extreme caution for outdoor work), in which months and from which hour, with a suggested work schedule. "Download report" produces a one-page report (four answers, chart, heat calendar, method, limits and NASA data links) that a community can attach to a grant application or send to its city hall, and "Download data" exports the annual series as CSV.

Case study: Boipeba Island, Bahia, Brazil Raízes do Futuro, winner of the UNICEF Brazil Youth Challenge Blockchain 2026, runs community waste collection on Boipeba, on foot and by boat. Using NASA POWER monthly, daily and hourly data we found:

  • Dangerous heat for outdoor work doubled: days with heat index at or above 32 °C (NWS "extreme caution") went from 64 to 132 a year (+37 days per decade, 95% CI +13 to +60, p = 0.005), with a change point after 2018.
  • The risky season grew from December to April to November to May. At noon in February and March, 3 in 4 days now reach extreme caution, against about 1 in 2 in 2001 to 2010.
  • Mean daily maximum rose from 28.3 °C (1981 to 1990) to 29.6 °C (2016 to 2025), +0.38 °C per decade. Hot days above the 1981 to 2010 90th percentile went from 24 to 110 a year, with a change point after 2004.
  • Where: warming is significant in all 18 unique NASA POWER cells of the Baixo Sul coast (+0.19 to +0.40 °C per decade).

Being honest about uncertainty NASA POWER shows annual rainfall at Boipeba falling from about 1,880 mm to about 910 mm. Reanalysis rainfall trends can carry artifacts, so we flag it as a signal to confirm with GPM IMERG and local gauges. Reanalysis cells (0.5° x 0.625°) mix island, sea and mainland and smooth the daily heat peak, so real heat on land is likely higher than shown. Duplicate grid cells are counted once. Trends are not forecasts.

Benefits and expected impact

  • Safer work: the hourly heat calendar becomes the collection schedule (finish routes by 8 a.m. from February to April and by 9 a.m. in the rest of the risky season, November to May) and a pause rule when the heat index forecast passes 32 °C.
  • Better funding decisions: NASA-backed trends, with stated uncertainty, help the project's Children's Fund and its partners prioritise climate adaptation for children's health and education.
  • Open for every community: the tool runs for any coordinates in a browser, with no installation and no login. Any cooperative, school or city hall can build its own heat calendar and download a report for grant applications, adaptation plans or ESG reporting today.
  • Next steps: validate rainfall with GPM IMERG, add sea surface temperature and sea level for coastal sites, and relate rainfall to the waste reaching mangroves and beaches using the project's collection records.

What already exists and what is new Climate trend tools already exist, mostly for researchers: the KNMI Climate Explorer computes trends and significance for any location, NOAA Climate at a Glance publishes regional time series, and Google Earth Engine or Climate Engine run Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope with an account and code. Our tool brings the same statistical rigour to any community without login or code, answers all four challenge questions plus "since when" in plain language, and turns the result into a concrete decision: when it is safe to work outdoors.

Tools and languages JavaScript, HTML and CSS (live tool, statistics in the browser), Leaflet and OpenStreetMap (map), Python with NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib (offline analysis and charts), NASA POWER API, GitHub and GitHub Pages, PptxGenJS (slides).
